issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: 'Never Alone' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence and the rest of the profile. This item more strongly suggests fear of being alone with a potentially abusive intimate or familiar person, whereas the threat items center on strangers and general vigilance. That mismatch is difficult to explain clinically within the same trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'Contamination' is not well aligned with the trauma type and accompanying appraisals. Feeling dirty or contaminated is more characteristic of sexual trauma; with police violence, and with the current memory/threat content, this appraisal stands out as clinically incongruent rather than merely unusual.

vignette:
David is a 58-year-old American dentist who came to treatment after several years of trying to narrow his life down to what felt manageable. He lives with his partner and still works, but in a more constricted way than before. The event he returns to began after an ordinary evening drive home. He had been pulled over by police, and what he remembers most sharply is how quickly the stop ceased to make sense to him. An officer approached his car, ordered him out, and before David could make sense of what was happening he was being shouted at, forced down, and struck. In his recollection, the scene is dominated by sound and impact: the barked commands in his ear, the hard, overwhelming noise of voices at close range, and the bodily pain where he was pinned and hit. Even now, when the memory comes back, he sometimes hears those sounds again in his head as if they are happening in the room with him, and he feels pain in the same places on his body that hurt that night. At the same time, he often speaks about the event in a detached way, as though it happened to another man. He can describe it, but the memory carries a strange unreal quality, and he has said that it feels alien, not fully his.

In the weeks afterward, David found himself preoccupied not only with what had happened but with what it meant about him. He had come to believe there was something about him that made the event happen, some quality in the way he looked, moved, or responded that had led the officers to target him. Alongside that was a fixed sense of violation: what happened had been profoundly unfair, and in his mind nothing meaningful had been done about it. He speaks about this with bitterness rather than outrage now, as if outrage would require energy he no longer has. More and more, he has felt that the life he had before was gone for good. When he says his life has been destroyed by the trauma, he does not mean that everything literally stopped; he means that the world he moved through with ease and assumption of ordinary safety no longer exists for him.

That shift has become visible in the smallest parts of his day. In public he monitors the space around him constantly, scanning entrances, faces, and body movements. What disturbs him most are strangers who come toward him in routine settings. A person crossing too directly in a parking lot, someone stepping up behind him at a coffee counter, a man moving toward him on the sidewalk can make his body tense before he has had time to think. He rarely sits anywhere without first deciding where the safest seat is. In restaurants he angles himself toward exits or walls; in waiting rooms he chooses places where no one can approach from behind. At the dental office this has become part of his working day. He notices who enters the reception area, where they stand, how close they come, and whether their tone shifts. If a new patient walks quickly toward him in the hallway, his attention locks onto the approach before he can return to whatever he was doing.

Over time David has tried to manage by shrinking away from anything that might stir him up. He avoids not only upsetting situations but also experiences that might bring any strong feeling, even positive ones. He turns down social invitations, skips gatherings with friends, and keeps celebrations muted because he does not want the lift or drop of emotion that might leave him feeling exposed. He also avoids stress wherever he can, postponing difficult conversations, cutting back parts of his schedule, and structuring his days around predictability. These choices make sense to him; he sees them as the only way to get through the day without becoming overwhelmed. But they have also narrowed his life with his partner, who has watched him become more absent and unreachable, and they have changed the atmosphere of his practice, where routines now revolve as much around what David can tolerate as around the needs of the office.

Sleep has become another battleground. He has trouble falling asleep and often staying asleep, lying alert to sounds in the house or replaying fragments of the event in the dark. By morning he is tired but already on guard. He finally sought help after recognizing that this way of living had become his entire life rather than a temporary adjustment. He was troubled by how automatically he now searches for danger and by how cut off he has become from other people and from himself. What frightens him most is the possibility that this is permanent—that the man who was pulled from his car is the only version of him left. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to feel that the memory belongs to him again without taking over every room he enters.
